title: How would you plan capacity for this service over the next year?
summary: Distinct from a sudden spike — tests whether you can build a growth-rate-driven plan with lead-time awareness for hardware and licensing, not just react when limits hit.

slides.markdown:
Planned growth is a different problem from a sudden spike. A spike is about surviving an unexpected step function in traffic right now; steady growth is about forecasting a curve months out and making sure capacity arrives *before* you cross your current ceiling.

The interviewer is testing whether you build a growth-rate-driven plan with real lead-time awareness — ordering hardware, getting budget approved, provisioning a managed database tier all take time — rather than reacting only once a dashboard turns red.

Ask what the historical growth rate actually is — a service growing 5% a quarter and one growing 30% a quarter need completely different planning horizons, and guessing instead of asking wastes the rest of the answer.

Ask what the lead time is to add capacity — hardware procurement, license approvals, or a managed vendor's own provisioning process. This is the number that decides *when* you need to act, not just *whether* you will — a service with a 2-quarter hardware lead time has to start the process 2 quarters before it actually needs the extra capacity, not the week it runs out.

Project forward from the historical growth rate to find when you'll cross current capacity, add a buffer for lead time, and set a trigger threshold that fires early enough to act before the crossing, not at it.

The trigger threshold is the operational piece that turns a forecast into a plan: instead of "we'll need more capacity sometime next year," it's "start procurement the moment utilization crosses 70%, because that's exactly lead-time-months before the projected ceiling."

```
Baseline: 90K QPS, growing 15%/quarter
Current ceiling: 140K QPS

Q1: 90K * 1.15 = 103.5K
Q2: 103.5K * 1.15 ≈ 119K
Q3: 119K * 1.15 ≈ 137K
Q4: 137K * 1.15 ≈ 157K   <- crosses 140K ceiling
```

Projecting a 15%/quarter growth rate against the current 140K ceiling shows the crossing lands in roughly 4 quarters. That's the "we need to act by" date — worked backward from when new capacity would actually be available, not forward from when you first notice you're close to full.

Current infra handles 100K QPS with 40% headroom, giving a 140K ceiling. At 15%/quarter growth from a 90K QPS baseline, you cross 140K in roughly 4 quarters. But ordering and provisioning new database read replicas takes 2 quarters of lead time.

The trigger to start that procurement needs to fire 2 quarters *before* the projected crossing — around quarter 2 — not at the crossing itself. Waiting until quarter 4 to start a 2-quarter procurement process means arriving 2 quarters late, with the ceiling already breached in the meantime.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: licensed and vendor-managed components
slides.markdown:
Different components have wildly different lead times, and the plan needs to account for each on its own terms. A managed database's tier upgrade might take just a support ticket and a scheduled maintenance window — days, not months. An on-prem hardware order might take a full procurement cycle with budget approval — a quarter or more.

A single growth curve can hide multiple different action dates once you break it down by component: the database might need action next month, while the load balancer's next tier has months of runway left. Treat each dependency's lead time separately rather than picking one blanket buffer for everything.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Provisioning ahead of the growth curve costs money sitting mostly idle in the meantime; provisioning right at the curve risks a capacity crunch if growth outpaces even a slightly optimistic forecast.

| Approach | Cost | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Provision well ahead (big buffer) | Higher — capacity sits underused for longer | Lower — cushion against forecast error |
| Provision right at the curve | Lower — less idle spend | Higher — any growth surprise causes a crunch |

The buffer size is a direct trade between idle cost and outage risk — there's no universally correct answer, only a deliberate choice based on how confident the forecast is and how expensive a crunch would be for this specific service.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: growth isn't linear — planning for an uncertain forecast
slides.markdown:
Plan against a range — conservative, expected, and aggressive growth curves — rather than trusting a single static projection for the full year. Set the action trigger off the more conservative curve, so you're not caught flat-footed if growth outpaces the middle-of-the-road estimate.

Revisit the forecast on a regular cadence — quarterly, say — rather than setting it once in January and assuming it still holds in October. A forecast is a living estimate, and the whole point of a trigger-based plan is that it can react to real data as it comes in, not just the guess made a year earlier. For the underlying estimation techniques, see [back-of-envelope estimation](back-of-envelope-fundamentals).

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: budget approval takes longer than the business will commit ahead
slides.markdown:
Build a more modular scaling path — smaller, more frequent capacity additions — so no single commitment has to be made as far ahead. Instead of one large 6-month-ahead approval for a year's worth of capacity, break it into smaller quarterly asks that each require less advance commitment.

This is explicitly a trade-off, not a free win: smaller, more frequent additions are usually less cost-efficient per unit of capacity than one large batched purchase. But it's often the only path available when the business genuinely won't commit budget far enough ahead to match your ideal lead time.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: waiting until 90% utilization to start the conversation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We're not out of capacity yet — let's start the capacity conversation once we're actually getting close."

**Why it's wrong:** if the component in question has a multi-quarter procurement lead time, waiting until 90% utilization to start guarantees you'll hit the ceiling before the new capacity arrives — the math simply doesn't have time to work out. The read-replica scenario in this topic is exactly this: starting at the crossing point instead of 2 quarters earlier means arriving 2 quarters too late.

**Correct model:** set the trigger to fire based on the *lead time*, not on how close you feel to the ceiling — for a long-lead-time component, that trigger point can look surprisingly early, like 60-70% utilization rather than 90%.

Project forward from the historical growth rate to find when you'll cross current capacity, then work backward from each component's actual lead time to set an action trigger that fires early enough — not at 90% utilization, but at whatever point gives the procurement process time to finish before the projected crossing.

Treat each dependency's lead time separately, since a managed database tier upgrade and an on-prem hardware order can differ by months. Plan against a range of growth curves rather than one static number, and if the business won't commit budget far enough ahead, shift to smaller, more frequent capacity additions instead.
